title: Episode 266: Susan B. Anthony: The Vote of 1872, the Trial of Rochester, and the 19th Amendment

The monumental, indomitable life of Susan Brownell Anthony: the Quaker schoolteacher from Massachusetts who became the undisputed general of the American women's suffrage movement. Forming an unbreakable fifty-year partnership with Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Anthony traveled tens of thousands of miles across frontier America by train, stagecoach, and sleigh, enduring mob violence and ridicule to demand the right to vote. In November 1872, Anthony boldly cast an illegal ballot in Rochester, New York, leading to a sensational federal trial where an authoritarian judge ordered the all-male jury to convict her without deliberation. Refusing to pay a single dollar of her fine, Anthony led the movement to the brink of victory, declaring in her final public speech that failure is impossible. Discover the champion of equality.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series honors the indefatigable champion of universal democracy: the Quaker reformer who dedicated half a century to winning the ballot for American women. Here is George with the courageous life of Susan B. Anthony.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE QUAKER FIRE OF ADAMS: 1820 TO 1845
Born in February 1820 in the shadow of Mount Greylock in Adams, Massachusetts, Susan Brownell Anthony was raised in a strict, devout Quaker family steeped in traditions of social equality, pacifism, and abolitionism. Her father Daniel was a cotton mill owner who treated male and female workers equally and refused to buy slave-grown cotton; her mother Lucy Read raised their children with an unshakeable sense of moral duty. Taught by her father that both boys and girls possessed an inner divine light that demanded education, Susan learned to read and write at age three. When her schoolmaster refused to teach her long division because she was a girl, her father pulled her out of school and established a home academy. Following the financial Panic of 1837, which wiped out the family fortune and forced them to auction their furniture, seventeen-year-old Susan began teaching at rural boarding academies, sending her earnings home to support her parents. Teaching in Canajoharie, New York, Susan was outraged to discover that female teachers were paid barely one-fourth the salary of male colleagues for identical work. Joining the Daughters of Temperance, she experienced her first bitter taste of public discrimination when she stood up to speak at a temperance convention in Albany, only to be rebuked by the male chairman: 'The sisters were not invited here to speak, but to listen and learn.'  Her father Daniel's unyielding principles left an indelible imprint upon Susan's moral character: he insisted on paying female mill operatives fair cash wages and strictly barred alcohol and card-playing from his home. Her years teaching at Canajoharie transformed her into an outspoken advocate for pedagogical reform, arguing before astonished male schoolboards that girls possessed identical mathematical and analytical capabilities as boys.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE MEETING OF THE MINDS: ANTHONY AND STANTON: MAY 1851
In May 1851, on a street corner in Seneca Falls, New York, Susan B. Anthony was introduced by fellow abolitionist Amelia Bloomer to Elizabeth Cady Stanton. It was the fateful catalyst of modern American social history: a legendary fifty-year intellectual and political partnership that transformed the republic. Stanton was a brilliant philosophical theorist, fiery speechwriter, and mother of seven children tied to her domestic household; Anthony was an unmarried, fearless executive organizer, orator, and field general who could travel unencumbered to every corner of the nation. Stanton later mused with affectionate wit: 'I forged the thunderbolts, and she fired them.' Together, they published the radical newspaper The Revolution, bearing the immortal motto: 'Men, their rights and nothing more; women, their rights and nothing less.' During the Civil War, they organized the Women's Loyal National League, gathering four hundred thousand signatures on petitions demanding the total abolition of slavery, providing critical political backing for Lincoln's Thirteenth Amendment.  The mutual devotion between Anthony and Stanton was reinforced by their complementary temperaments: when Stanton was exhausted by the care of her young children, Anthony would arrive at Seneca Falls, rock the babies, bake bread, and manage household chores so Stanton could write undisturbed in her study. Their radical weekly journal The Revolution tackled taboo topics of marriage reform, unequal divorce laws, and equal pay for female factory laborers, challenging the Victorian cult of domesticity at its very foundations.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE BALLOT OF NOVEMBER 5, 1872: VOTING IN ROCHESTER
Following the ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment in 1868, which guaranteed citizenship and equal protection of the laws to all persons born in the United States, Anthony and Stanton developed a bold legal strategy: if women were citizens, they were constitutionally entitled to the supreme privilege of citizenship—the ballot. On Friday, November 1, 1872, fifty-two-year-old Susan B. Anthony strode into a barber shop in Rochester's Eighth Ward with her three sisters, demanding that the young election inspectors register them to vote under the Fourteenth Amendment. Reading the constitutional clauses aloud and citing the New York election code, Anthony stared down the hesitant young poll inspectors until they relented. On Tuesday, November 5, Anthony cast her vote in the presidential election between Ulysses S. Grant and Horace Greeley. That evening, she wrote an ecstatic letter to Stanton: 'Well I have been & gone & done it!!—positively voted the Republican ticket—straight... If only now—all the women would do the same!'  When Anthony entered the election registration office at the barbershop on West Main Street, the young election inspector Beverly W. Jones initially protested that voting rolls were strictly restricted to male citizens under New York state law. Brandishing her well-worn copy of the United States Constitution, Anthony read aloud the newly ratified Fourteenth Amendment, demanding: 'Are we persons? Are we citizens? Does not the Constitution declare that no State shall make or enforce any law which shall abridge the privileges of citizens?' Shaken by her legal precision, Jones and his fellow inspectors swore in the women and recorded their names.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: UNITED STATES V. SUSAN B. ANTHONY: JUNE 1873
Thirteen days later, a handsome federal deputy marshal knocked on Anthony's front door with a federal warrant, arresting her for the crime of 'voting without having a lawful right to vote'. Refusing to pay her bail, Anthony spent the months leading up to her trial traveling across twenty-nine towns in Monroe and Ontario counties, delivering her electrifying address: 'Is It a Crime for a Citizen of the United States to Vote?' In June 1873, at the courthouse in Canandaigua, New York, Associate Justice Ward Hunt presided over United States v. Susan B. Anthony. In an outrageous subversion of constitutional due process, Judge Hunt refused to allow Anthony to testify, pulled a pre-written opinion from his robe, and ordered the all-male jury to deliver a directed verdict of guilty without leaving their seats or speaking a word. When Hunt asked the prisoner if she had anything to say why sentence should not be pronounced, Anthony rose like an avenging angel, delivering the most devastating indictment of judicial tyranny in American history: 'Yes, your honor, I have many things to say; for in your ordered verdict of guilty, you have trampled under foot every vital principle of our government. My natural rights, my civil rights, my political rights, my judicial rights, are all alike ignored.'  The presiding judge, Ward Hunt, was a staunch political ally of Republican Senator Roscoe Conkling, leader of the New York political machine that feared an independent female electorate would disrupt machine politics. By refusing to permit the jury to deliberate and directly instructing the court clerk to enter a guilty verdict, Hunt violated the ancient Sixth Amendment guarantee of trial by jury in criminal prosecutions, sparking blistering editorials even from conservative legal journals across the nation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: 'NOT A PENNY SHALL GO TO THIS UNJUST PENALTY'
As Judge Hunt repeatedly pounded his gavel and shouted for the prisoner to sit down, Anthony refused to be silenced, recounting how women were denied the right to be tried by a jury of their peers, denied political representation, and taxed without consent. When Hunt finally fined her one hundred dollars plus the costs of prosecution, Anthony defiantly proclaimed: 'May it please your honor, I shall never pay a dollar of your unjust penalty. All the stock in trade I possess is a ten thousand dollar debt, incurred by publishing my paper—The Revolution... And I shall earnestly and persistently continue to urge all women to the practical recognition of the old revolutionary maxim, that 'Resistance to tyranny is obedience to God.' Cunningly, Judge Hunt declined to commit her to prison until the fine was paid, depriving Anthony of the legal ability to appeal her case to the United States Supreme Court. The fine was never paid, and the federal government never dared attempt to collect it.  Anthony's refusal to surrender to judicial extortion established an enduring precedent of civil disobedience that later inspired twentieth-century civil rights activists. When the court bailiffs hesitated to take her into physical custody, Judge Hunt realized that sending Anthony to jail would enable her defense counsel, former federal judge Henry R. Selden, to file a writ of habeas corpus directly to the United States Supreme Court, exposing his illegal directed verdict to federal constitutional review.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: FIFTY YEARS ON THE SUFFRAGE TRAIL: 1875 TO 1900
For the next three decades, Anthony was the unstoppable locomotive of the suffrage movement. Traveling up to ten thousand miles a year, she gave over one hundred lectures annually, crossing the snowy prairies of Wyoming, Kansas, California, and Oregon. She slept in drafty frontier cabins, rode in open wagons through blizzards, and faced down hostile mobs throwing rotten eggs and insults. In 1878, Anthony convinced California Senator Aaron Sargent to introduce a federal constitutional amendment guaranteeing that the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. For forty-two years, that exact text was reintroduced into every single session of Congress, becoming affectionately known across the nation as the 'Susan B. Anthony Amendment'. In 1890, Anthony united competing suffrage factions into the National American Woman Suffrage Association, serving as its president until age eighty. When asked if she ever regretted remaining unmarried, she replied with serene dignity: 'I never found the man who was necessary to my happiness. I was very well as I was.'  Her tireless travels took her to the rough mining camps of Colorado, the frontier sod houses of Nebraska, and the logging settlements of Oregon, where she spoke in drafty barns, saloon billiard rooms, and railway depots. Often surviving on crackers and cold tea, Anthony faced howling mobs hurling rotten eggs and burning her in effigy, yet she never raised her voice in anger, meeting hostility with calm logic, constitutional legal analysis, and disarming humor.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: 'FAILURE IS IMPOSSIBLE': THE NINETEENTH AMENDMENT
In February 1906, eighty-six-year-old Susan B. Anthony attended her final suffrage convention in Washington. Standing before thousands of cheering women, frail and suffering from heart disease, Anthony delivered her final public words to the movement: 'Failure is impossible!' One month later, on March 13, 1906, Anthony passed away peacefully in her bed in Rochester. Fourteen years after her death, on August 18, 1920, the Nineteenth Amendment was officially ratified, enshrining equal voting rights for women into the supreme law of the land. In 1979, the United States Mint honored her memory on the Susan B. Anthony one-dollar coin, making her the first non-presidential historical woman featured on circulating U.S. currency. On Election Day in 2016 and 2020, tens of thousands of women made pilgrimages to Mount Hope Cemetery in Rochester, placing their 'I Voted' stickers across her marble headstone in silent gratitude. Susan B. Anthony remains an eternal beacon of democratic courage: the woman who demanded nothing less than full equality, proving that perseverance in the cause of justice will always triumph in the end.  At the National American Woman Suffrage Association convention in Washington, D.C., in February 1906, eighty-six-year-old Anthony stood before thousands of cheering women for the final time. Leaning heavily on the arm of her protege Carrie Chapman Catt, her voice clear and resonant despite physical frailness, she exhorted the younger generation never to surrender the fight until universal enfranchisement was won. Fourteen years after her death, on August 26, 1920, the Nineteenth Amendment was officially certified, forever enshrining the principle that the right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 269: Elizabeth Cady Stanton—The Declaration of Sentiments, the Solitude of Self, and the Woman's Bible. Until then, stay curious.
